title: A surprising discovery about the possibility of extraterrestrial life.
excerpt: New discoveries by scientists suggest that icy moons around giant planets could become attractive candidates in the search for extraterrestrial life.
content:
A new study suggests that icy moons in the Solar System may still maintain oceans of liquid water beneath their icy surface even after suffering massive collisions powerful enough to shatter them.

This discovery could open up new approaches in the search for extraterrestrial life .

Frozen worlds may conceal oceans.

Many moons orbiting Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are believed to be concealing oceans of liquid water deep beneath kilometers of ice.

Liquid water is one of the fundamental components essential for life as we know it, making these icy worlds promising targets in the hunt for extraterrestrial life.

Notably, the regions around these giant planets have experienced countless violent collisions. Scientists suspect that some of the moons we see today may be remnants of massive impacts, having been repeatedly shattered by other celestial bodies and then reassembled under the influence of gravity.

This raises a crucial question for astrobiology: Could massive collisions destroy the moon's inner ocean, thereby extinguishing any chance of life?

A study led by the University of Maryland, published in the journal Nature Astronomy, sought to answer this question.

Scientists simulated the process by which a moon is destroyed, reformed, and continues to evolve over billions of years.

"The big question we asked was whether these destructive events helped the moon form oceans afterward, or whether they wiped out the oceans and turned the moon back into a cold, dead world," explains Marc Neveu, lead author of the study and research astronomer at the University of Maryland.

The results were quite surprising: "Those major collisions don't seem to actually determine the existence of the ocean. If the ocean existed before the collision, it's highly likely that it still existed after the collision, and vice versa."

While collisions don't necessarily determine whether a moon has oceans, the enormous amount of heat generated by the impact can still leave a noticeable mark on its surface.

Rhea, one of Saturn's medium-sized moons, is a particularly noteworthy case. Some of the ancient impact craters on Rhea look unusual, with a rather smooth and soft shape rather than the sharp edges of newer craters.

Researchers suggest this could be a sign that a past collision heated the ocean below, causing the ice sheet to change.

Neveu likened this phenomenon to someone building a snowman in winter, but a week later the weather warms up and the snowman begins to melt.

The craters on Rhea also appear to have been "softened" in a similar way, the only difference being that the heat source doesn't come from the Sun but from within the moon itself.

An ancient collision that increased the temperature of the inner ocean may explain Rhea's distinctive appearance today.

Even a torn-apart moon can still become an ocean world.

To understand what happens billions of years after a collision, scientists cannot simply simulate the moment of impact.

Neveu and his colleagues at the Southwest Research Institute in Colorado, USA, and the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel combined the collision model with a separate model simulating the evolutionary process inside the moon.

Collision simulations track millions of pieces of rock and ice as they are crushed, heated, and then reassembled.

The research team examined moons with radii of approximately 500km and 1,000km, which were struck by smaller celestial bodies with enough energy to shatter them.

"These were almost the biggest collisions we could imagine. If even these didn't make a significant difference, it's highly unlikely that smaller collisions would either," Neveu said.

After the moon reformed, the model continued to track it for about 4.5 billion years. Scientists calculated the amount of heat accumulating and escaping from the core, and determined whether the ice could melt to form a liquid water ocean.

The results showed that the impact of the collision depended significantly on the size of the moon.

On large moons, the energy from the collision could be converted into additional heat, potentially making existing oceans thicker and maintaining their liquid state for billions of years.

But with smaller moons, the situation is reversed. Before impact, they may have possessed a composite outer layer of ice and rock, acting as an "insulating blanket" to trap heat inside and sustain the ocean.

When a massive impact breaks this structure, the moon reformes with rocks sinking to the core and ice rising to the surface. As the natural insulation disappears, the smaller moon has a harder time retaining heat, and the oceans also struggle to survive.

However, the important point is that in both cases, the collision did not create an ocean that would not have existed in the first place. In other words, a moon does not naturally become an ocean world simply because it is shattered.

Tides can also determine life.

In addition to collisions, heat generated by tidal forces also plays a crucial role in maintaining liquid water beneath the ice.

When gravity distorts a moon as it orbits its host planet, internal friction can generate heat.

According to Neveu, this factor is at least as important as the collision history when assessing a moon's potential to support life.

The orbits of the moons can also change over time, even placing them in orbits where collisions are likely to occur.

Therefore, to reconstruct the history of a lunar system, scientists need to connect its movements with the changes occurring deep beneath the surface.

Neveu said he wants to go further by simulating an entire lunar system, observing how they move, collide, and change their internal structure over time.

This approach could help scientists reconstruct what happened around Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

These "reincarnated worlds" become targets for the search for life.

The new discovery has implications for a host of moons that NASA and other space agencies are interested in. These include Saturn's Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, and Rhea; Uranus' Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon; and Neptune's Triton, its largest moon.

Identifying which worlds are most likely to possess liquid water will help scientists select targets for future exploration missions and determine what equipment spacecraft should carry.

A buried ocean can be detected through its gravitational influence. On the surface, salt layers or ice volcanoes erupting material from within, known as cryovolcanoes, can also provide important clues.

In particular, the scale of hypothetical life beneath the ice will determine how scientists design the search mission.

"If there were only a few bacteria, you wouldn't design the search mission the same way you would for an ocean teeming with whales," Neveu said. "The type of life we ​​want to find will determine the type of tools we need to develop."

This discovery therefore shows not only that moons can "survive" terrible space catastrophes.

More importantly, it suggests that a world that has been destroyed and reformed could continue to nurture conditions suitable for life for billions of years.

This makes icy moons around giant planets more attractive than ever in the hunt for extraterrestrial life.

(According to SciTechDaily, Earthsky, iflscience)
